Sir,

At 2.25 p.m. a telephone message from C.P.C. 2021
reported a shooting affray on Great Western Road near
Lane 52 A.

Station alarm was sounded and a large party of
Police turned out under Officer i/c when it was ascertai-
ned members of the Japanese Gendarmerie had been fired
upon and they returned the fire.

A call was put into the Reserve Unit which turned
out under Inspector Campbell.

Barrier duties on Settlement Boundary were doubled.

Investigations ascertained that two members of the
Japanese Gendarmerie were proceeding from East to West
along the North footpath of Great Western Road at about
2.20 p.m. When passing Lane 52 A (Wang Ka Loong 汪家弄)
an unidentified gunman emerged from the Lane and opened
fire on the soldiers seriously wounding Lance Corporal
Mitsuhei Onaga. The wounded man fell into the doorway
of a small shop No. I 471 Great Western Road which is on
the West corner of Lane 52 A. No blood stains are
visible, but vomit is visible inside the doorstep.

The uninjured Gendarme swung round and apparently
sighted the criminal take cover round the corner of the
Lane. The soldier, Lance Corporal Hito, ran East about
twelve yards and apparently took cover in a doorway of
House 50 Great Western Road and being armed with a rifle
exchanged shots with the assassin. One rifle shot having
struck the pillar of a gate at the rear of shop I. 471

On the West corner of Lane 524 an open shoe-
repairer's stall is situated and at the time of the

DEC 20 1940

Japanese Road
Work Continues

Rain Fails To Halt
Project; Nomura
Funeral Held

The Japanese authorities today were still busy with the construction of the projected highway from Great Western Road to Yu Yuen Road, despite the slight rainfall this morning which slowed down the work.

Similarly, construction was proceeding in the widening of a lane along Thorburn Road where last week a Japanese medical officer Surgeon-Lieutenant Masao Nomura was shot by a gunman who was later reported to have been apprehended by the Japanese Naval Landing Party authorities.

Services Held

Memorial services for the late medical officer, who was shot dead while vaccinating Chinese on Ward Road, near Thorburn Road, were held yesterday afternoon at the Nishi-Honganji Temple, Chapoo Road, at noon yesterday.

The services were attended by high-ranking Japanese officials and prominent Japanese businessmen here. Following the services for Surgeon-Lieutenant Nomura a special service for other war dead of the Japanese Expeditionary Forces in Central China was held at the Nishi-Honganji Temple.

Officials Silent

Meanwhile, today, Japanese naval quarters here continued to maintain silence regarding the Chinese who was reported to have been arrested last week following the slaying of Surgeon-Lieutenant Masao Nomura.

It is learned that the arrest was carried out by the Japanese Naval Landing Party at a small Chinese village on Chining Road, near Thorburn Road, after thorough searches had been conducted in the area for more than 24 hours by the Japanese authorities.

Blockade free

（印：SHANGHAI MUNICIPAL POLICE SPECIAL BRANCH）

Public Nervous
Buses Resume
Normal Runs
In W. District

With the resumption of normal bus and tram transportation, conditions in the western district yesterday had practically returned to normal.

Only a small section of Edinburgh Road was still barricaded. Motorists and pedestrians going north from Avenue Haig found barricades on the south side of the Great Western Road junction.

Pedestrians for a time made use of an alley which runs parallel to Great Western Road northward from Edinburgh Road but when city government discovered the detour, this alley was also barricaded.

An official of the China General Omnibus Company told The China Press that all lines were making their normal runs into the once blockaded area, although the shuttle bus from St. George's to Jessfield was maintained until a late hour in the afternoon.

Although the weather was warm and the sun was bright, visitors at the Jessfield Park were few, apparently due to the fact that residents here have not gotten over their nervousness.

Settlement rickshas, however, were still banned from the district. City government police were seen standing guard at all important street entrances leading from the Settlement and Concession into the western district ordering the vehicles to keep out.

Million Dollar
Squeeze Raises
Badland Barrier

Gambling Dens Offer
Funds As “Fine;”
New Road Built

The sum of $1,000,000 was obtained by the Japanese Gendarmerie in the western area from Chinese gambling dens and other “interests” in the district as a “fine” toward lifting the blockade, it was reliably learned this morning.

It is understood that the major part of the “fine” was paid by the China Club gambling house, which reportedly paid $300,000 while the additional amount was “subscribed” to by several other gaming dens and several other public enterprises in the western district.

Japanese Road Building

This morning the Japanese authorities in the area were busily engaged in the construction of a new thoroughfare linking Great Western Road with Yu Yuen Road, the project cutting through from Great Western Road from the spot where Private Sazaki of the Japanese gendarmerie was shot a little over two weeks ago.

High wooden gates, painted white, were being placed this morning at the Great Western Road opening of the new road, and it is believed that a permanent guard of Japanese military or Chinese municipality police will be stationed at this point.

Named For Soldier

The new road when completed will be named after Private Sazaki, it is learned, and will be about 40 feet wide. It will be linked to a new thoroughfare which the Japanese are planning from Jessfield Road, where nearly two months ago Corporal Sato was shot.

The latter roadway will be named Corporal Sato and will lead from the Japanese gendarme headquarters at 94 Jessfield Road, around Kinnear Road, and through to Yu Yuen Road, between Tifeng and Edinburgh Roads.

Houses Torn Down

A large number of Chinese houses in the vicinity of Jessfield Road have already been torn down to enable the construction of the road to be named after Corporal Sato. Two-week Old Western Area
Blockade Lifted Yesterday

Buses, Trams Allowed to Run in Yu Yuen Road
Following the Removal of Barricades

ONE of the longest blockades, imposed by the Japanese authorities on any district in Shanghai, ended yesterday at about noon when all the barriers in Great Western, Yu Yuen and Tifeng Roads were removed, allowing free traffic in the Western Area for the first time in exactly two weeks.

The removal of the barricades saw vehicles of the China General Omnibus Company and trolley buses of the Shanghai Tramways operate in Yu Yuen Road and Amherst Avenue. The Japanese buses, which ran in the restricted area, have been taken off.

It was believed yesterday that other barriers placed by the Japanese authorities and members of the Shanghai Special Municipality Police would be removed in the near future. Some of these had been placed in Singapore, Connaught, Kiaochow and other boundary roads just a few days ago.

Although there is no official confirmation, it is believed that the Japanese authorities have arrested several suspects. The very first day of the blockade, on November 30, the Japanese arrested nine Chinese, while, one Russian of poor class was also detained by them. These arrests were all effected in Great Western Road, just a few steps from the spot where the unidentified gunman shot the Japanese gendarme.

That the blockade would be lifted in the very near future was predicted by the Japanese Embassy spokesman, who added that the barricades would be removed as soon as the Japanese authorities would end their investigations.

The restrictions were slightly relaxed on Thursday evening when the Japanese authorities removed the barriers in Great Western Road and lifted the curfew.

The blockade, the longest ever suffered by this city, started shortly after 2 p.m. on November 30 when Private Sazaki of the Japanese Gendarmerie was shot by a Chinese gunman just outside Lane 52 in Great Western Road. The other Japanese gendarme, in whose company the victim was at the time of the shooting, attempted to bring the culprit down and fired several shots at him, none of which had taken any effect. The wounded gendarme was taken to the Country Hospital, but was later removed by the Japanese to Hongkew. On the way there, he died. Dr. D. W. Nance, who treated the wounded gendarme when he was brought to the hospital, stated that an operation would have saved his life if it had been performed on the spot.

Following the shooting of Sazaki, the Japanese closed all the entrances into the area, not allowing even foreigners to pass through. The conditions in the district became serious as a shortage of foodstuffs began to be felt. The severe restrictions imposed by them hit all the residents in the area, foreigners being inconvenienced in a big way, school children and teachers finding themselves in difficulties on several occasions, while five foreign women and eighty Chinese operators were stranded in the Lucerne Exchange in Edinburgh Road for several days.

Later, Mr. Poul Scheel, senior consul here, made representations to the Japanese Consul-General, resulting in the relaxation of restrictions in the area, although buses and trams were not allowed to run in Yu Yuen Road. The Japanese, instead, started running their own buses and explained this by stating that they wished to prevent inconvenience to people in the area, and adding that the measure was only a temporary one.

Representations

The China General Omnibus Company and the Shanghai Tramways, nevertheless, protested to the Shanghai Municipal Council, and the latter made representations to the Japanese authorities. No reply, however, had been received by the Council.

Yesterday, the Shanghai Municipal Council made further representations to the Japanese Consul-General over the conditions arising out of the blockade in the Western Area, drawing the attention of the Japanese Consul-General to the interference with watchmen employed in the area and to the irregularity of the requirements that rickshaws operating in the Council's roads must obtain Chinese licences.

The attack on Private Sazaki was the twelfth made on Japanese nationals since September 26 when Major Isebe was mortally wounded while walking in North Szechuen Road. All with the exception of three were carried out in the Hongkew District. One of the assaults took place in the Siccawei Sector while the other two in the Western Area, the first being the assassination of Corporal Sato of the Western Area Gendarmerie.

It was learned yesterday that the gambling houses, some of which had been forced to close up because of the restrictions imposed, would open their doors this evening.

OFF THE RECORD

Children . . . What Next?
AN eye-witness told OFF THE RECORD yesterday that following the discovery of the anti-Japanese posters in the blockaded area a number of children, around 10 years old, were arrested by Japanese gendarmes and Chinese policemen. The only reason for the arrests given by the Chinese policemen was that the posters, judging from the uncultivated style of the calligraphy, were believed to have been written by youngsters of tender age.
When reports that the children had been arrested reached the unblockaded area in the western district, rumors followed that if the writers of the posters could not be found the Japanese would round up all the children in areas adjoining the lane where the posters were discovered. Thus far, nothing of the kind has yet happened although the hunt for the 'culprits' were still on.

Check & Double Check
Under the usual slogan, "Impartial Not Neutral," a British contemporary came out a few days ago with an editorial asserting—in fact, doubly asserting—that Santi Quaranta had been occupied by the Italians. This was allegedly backed up by "a Greek claim," and "a Reuter report." Said the morning paper:—"The Greek claim from Athens to the effect that Santi Quaranta on the Albanian coast has been occupied by the Italians, is supported by a report carried by Reuters to the effect that the Italians are retreating along the coast...."
Which reminds us that journalistic sabotage has been rampant in Shanghai of late. About a week ago somebody inserted into an advertisement in Wang Ching-wei's paper, the Central China Daily News, a startling remark about Mr. Wang. Wednesday night Evepost Newscaster Sam Titlebaum, broadcasting over the Evepost station, denounced the Evening Post as having yielded to pressure of Tokyo, Berlin, or the entire Axis all at once. Sam's contract, prior to that, had been cancelled.

Employee Bites Employer
Further, on "Fifth" or "Eighth" columns, when employee bites employer—even though only figuratively and over the air—that should be news by a classical definition. But not for our contemporary, the Evepost, and hippo-hided publisher of the same, George Bruce. All English-speaking Shanghai is still talking of Sam Titlebaum's Wednesday night broadcast on the Post's own radio hour, excoriating his employers for allegedly yielding to Tokyo and/or Berlin pressure, but there's not a word in yesterday's Evepost about it. Evidently, Publisher Bruce's attitude is that of Clark Gable in a scene in "Idiot's Delight"—"I shall treat this outburst with the silent contempt that it deserves." Anyway, Gable mentioned the matter; our Mr. Bruce doesn't.

Western District Blockade
Continued by Japanese

Search for Slayer of Japanese Gendarme Believed
Unsuccessful ; Police Driver Injured by Soldier

SHANGHAI'S western "badlands" continued to remain under
blockade yesterday, with whole sections of Great Western,
Yu Yuen and Jessfield Roads being completely barred to Chinese
pedestrians, although foreigners were allowed to enter and leave
the area for a time. At 4.45 p.m., however, full restrictions were
again enforced, and no one, including foreigners, was permitted

blockaded area extended from Tifeng Road, with restrictions being
lighter beyond Edinburgh Road.

These measures, taken by the
Japanese authorities following the
shooting of another Japanese in
Great Western Road on Saturday
afternoon, were started soon after
the shooting, when Japanese gen-
darmes and members of Shanghai
Special Municipality Police rushed to
the scene and erected barbed wire
barricades across all roads leading
westward. No one, including for-
eigners, was allowed to leave or enter
the districts under search, although
later in the night foreigners were
allowed to proceed on foot along
Great Western Road.

The restrictions in the western
area were the cause of an incident
this morning, resulting in injuries to
a police driver, who was later sent
to the Police Hospital in Ward Road,
suffering from contusions of the thigh.
The trouble began shortly after 10
a.m. in Edinburgh Road and was a
result of language misunderstanding.
A police driver parked his car at a
certain spot in Edinburgh Road, just
as he was directed to do so by a
Japanese gendarme. Another gen-
darme, however, ordered him to re-
move the vehicle to another place,
and when the driver hesitated, not
understanding what was wanted of
him, he was hit in the thigh with the
butt of a rifle, causing him to sustain
serious injury to his thigh. An am-
bulance was immediately called out
and the unfortunate man was taken
to hospital.

The restrictions on traffic in the

Every endeavour will be made to

usual early hour, but if this should
be impossible a later delivery will
be made.

The continued blockade threw the

Road. The prospect of such a

The barricades have, since Satur-

Chinese residents in the district

Many foreigners living in the
Western district were unable to get
to their homes from the city. Those
returning late from cinemas and
places of amusement were forced to
take some round-about route to get
home, other returning to stay with
friends within the Settlement.

BADLANDS' BARRICADE

For the second time in two months the Japanese have barricaded the area just outside the western boundaries of the International Settlement. On Saturday one of three Japanese gendarmes who were shot at by a man alleged to be a Chinese gunman was injured and sent to hospital for treatment. It was subsequently rumoured that he had died from his injuries. Be that as it may from Saturday the outside area has been barricaded off, and the movements of thousands of residents, Chinese as well as foreign have been greatly hindered if not actually held up. It is difficult to get food into the area, while there are cases reported in which persons seriously sick have been denied that daily treatment upon which their very lives may depend. Children were prevented from going to school, though it is reported that this has since been rectified, and in general a state of complete inconvenience has been brought about, which reflects no credit whatever upon those authorities who have usurped the policing of the area in question.

The barricades have apparently been put into operation to prevent the wanted gunman from escaping from the district. There is no indication whatever that similar barricades have been placed on the western boundaries of the badlands, and if they had, that would not prevent the wanted man from escaping westwards across country. It must surely be apparent to all concerned that if the gunman remained in the area surrounding the scene of the crime any longer than it took him to get away, the man would be an utter fool. That is about the last charge which could be laid against these political assassins. The speed with which they get away from the scenes of their crimes is one of the features of their activities, and if the wanted man on this occasion was anywhere near the scene of the crime when the blockade was instituted it will indeed be surprising. Consequently the whole process, no matter how much it may commend itself to the authorities supposed to be policing the badlands, is a bad one, affording little chance for the capture of the guilty, and subjecting large numbers of people, in no way connected with the crime, to very considerable hardship.

The fact that this is the second of such crimes perpetrated against the Japanese gendarmerie within two months in this particular area suggests that the policing which is at present being carried out is as inefficient as the means adopted to catch the criminal. The state of the badlands is notorious and has been so for a very long time past. Despite efforts on the part of the Shanghai Municipal Council to co-operate with the outside authorities in endeavouring to restore that area to some semblance of law and order, despite the long drawn out negotiations for the establishment of a special police force to take care of the district, nothing tangible has been done up to the present, save to arrive at an agreement in principle with the late Mayor Fu Siao-en which has not yet been implemented.

No one has been more direct in its condemnation of political assassinations, whether the victims be high or low than this journal. Their utter futility is apparent to everyone save those criminally minded who still fancy that murder is a valuable political weapon, which it has been proved time out of number not to be. But these killings and attempted killings will continue until definite action is taken against those rogues who infest this particular Alsatia, no matter what their political affiliations may happen to be. There is consequently laid upon the shoulders of the administration of Greater Shanghai, and the Japanese gendarmerie responsibilities which they have assumed up to the present with no great display of efficiency. The way has been cleared for mutual co-operation between the authorities of the International Settlement and the outside areas, and advantage should be taken of the fact by proceeding with the establishment of the special force which has been agreed upon. The badlands are in great need of a thorough cleaning up, and the Japanese gendarmes and the Ta Tao police cannot hope ever to have the situation there well in hand until that has been done. Blockades and the like neither help to prevent crime nor apprehend the guilty and the sooner more efficient measures are devised the quicker will the authorities succeed in getting the situation under control.

Western Area Restrictions
Relaxed by Japanese

Passes Required for Foreigners Entering
Blockaded Zone ; Conference Takes Place

FOREIGNERS breathed more freely yesterday when it was learned that some relaxation of restrictions imposed by the Japanese authorities in the "badlands" following the shooting of a gendarme on Saturday had been obtained from the Japanese by the Consular Body. Mr. Poul Scheel, senior consul here, conferred with Mr. Tateki Horiuchi, Japanese Consul-General, yesterday afternoon when viewpoints were exchanged by the two officials.

In his meeting with the Japanese Consul-General, Mr. Scheel, it is understood, conveyed the Consular Body's regrets and condemnation of terrorism against Japanese subjects, but stated that he hoped that the blockade would be lifted as soon as possible, adding that foreigners in the area had been inconvenienced by the measures undertaken by the Japanese. Mr. Scheel asked that the Japanese should be as discreet as possible in their searches of foreigners and their cars, since the majority of the foreigners in the district enjoyed extraterritorial rights and were not subject to searches. The Japanese authorities were also asked to allow medical practitioners, school children and food suppliers in and out of the area.

It was learned that Mr. Horiuchi stated that the Japanese had no intention of causing harm to foreigners in that area, but that they were left without an alternative. He added that the blockade would be maintained until the time the Japanese are satisfied that searches are no longer required. These have been going for more than three days, during which time, according to certain reliable sources, more than one hundred Chinese were arrested. With regard to searching foreigners' cars, the Japanese Consul-General regretted the fact, but said that it had to be done, since the Japanese claim that the Chinese gunmen have been known to secrete their weapons in stationary cars, without the knowledge of either the chauffeurs or owners, retrieving them later by remembering the number of the vehicle. This was the reason why the cars had been searched by the Japanese. These measures, although regretted by the Japanese officials, were essential in order to carry out searches in the area, and would be continued until every bit of the district was thoroughly looked into.

Nevertheless, foreigners residing in the "badlands" would have to follow closely certain regulations laid down by the authorities in order to be allowed to pass in and out of the area now blockaded by a unit of the Japanese Gendarmerie.

The new regulations, it was learned, came into effect yesterday and were put into force in order to prevent the inconvenience which has been felt by the residents in the area. The regulations concern the area in the Western District, encompassed by Edinburgh, Yu Yuen, Tifeng and Great Western Roads.

It was learned that within the area restricted to the inner sides of Yu Yuen Road and Great Western Road, homes and houses facing the roads ramped, and both sides of Edinburgh Road, are considered blockaded. The areas outside the blockaded sector as defined, and inside the four roads, are considered restricted.

To pass in and out of the restricted zone, it was learned yesterday, Tifeng Road is open to foreigners at all hours. All traffic, however, must pass by an examining post situated at a spot between Bubbling Well Road and Avenue Foch. Automobiles driven by Chinese chauffeurs, but with no Chinese passengers, are allowed to pass the post.

Although rickshaw traffic inside the zone is allowed, such vehicles will be prohibited from passing out through the post. It is understood that arrangements for Chinese are also made at other points. The question of supplying food to Chinese residents in the blockaded and restricted areas is being considered by the Japanese authorities.

This last point has been the hardest felt during the blockade as all the rice has been bought up. It was learned yesterday that eggs are sold at eighty cents each, while meat was offered at as much as three dollars for a pound. The price of briquette coal has also risen considerably and only thirty balls are given for a dollar. This is the coal that is so much in use by Chinese housewives.

Special Passes

Residents of the blockaded area are, in general, not allowed to come out of the sector. It was pointed out, however, that foreigners in the area might be furnished with special passes by the unit on patrol, and with this they may pass through the post situated near the corner of Great Western and Edinburgh Roads, or at some other point so as to ultimately gain access to the post. It was further learned that only foreign residents in the blockaded area will be allowed to return to their residences. The numerous Chinese, working in downtown offices and living in the area, will have to continue to sleep at their friends or relatives' homes in other parts of the Settlement.

In the event of residents encountering difficulties, it is suggested that any such person get in direct contact with the Western Branch of the Japanese Gendarmerie at 84 Jessfield Road.

Meanwhile, it was learned that Private Sazaki, who was shot by the Chinese gunman on Saturday afternoon, succumbed to his wounds the same day on the way to Hongkew where he was being removed from the Country Hospital.

Dr. D. W. Nance, who treated the wounded soldier when he was brought to the Country Hospital, was reported to have stated that the gendarme's life might have been saved had an immediate operation been done. The Japanese authorities, however, arrived at the hospital soon after and ordered the man to be removed to Hongkew.

S.M.C. Communique

Earlier in the day, the Shanghai Municipal Council issued a communique, the full text of which was as follows:—

"Every effort has been and is being made by the Commissioner of Police and other Police Officers to secure a relaxation of the restrictions by direct negotiations with the Japanese authorities. The Senior Consul has also been requested to use his influence to the same end."

Questioned on the issue, a high Police official stated yesterday that the Police on their part could do little to obtain relaxation of the restrictions. The area, blockaded by the Japanese, was extended by them to the Paramount Hotel yesterday morning and soldiers and members of the Shanghai Special Municipality Police continued their patrols in the district, preventing Chinese from leaving and entering the area. Food supplies, however, were allowed in later in the morning, and bread and milk were brought there through Edinburgh Road. Schoolchildren and teachers were unhampered in entering the blockaded district.

Some foreigners, when questioned on the restrictions, stated that it was not the hardship that they felt, but the inconvenience. Newspapers and food could not be obtained there, while in some cases foreigners in private cars were detained for many minutes before the Japanese allowed them to pass.

The isolated eighty-five telephone operators, including five foreign women, were finally relieved yesterday morning, after being "marooned" at the Lucerne Telephone Exchange in Edinburgh Road for more than sixty hours. Their places were taken by a new shift and they went home to get the much needed rest.

The area was left without electric light for more than one hour yesterday morning when wire was cut and stolen by thieves. Notwithstanding all the restrictions, night life in the area west of the blockaded zone continued as entrance could be gained through Kinnear Road to Yu Yuen Road.

It was announced by the Settlement police yesterday afternoon that the barriers placed between Great Western and Tifeng Roads had been removed and that foreigners travelling in private cars or on foot might proceed to Great Western Road or Yu Yuen Road by this route.

"Guarantors" for Chinese

It was learned last night that the Chinese police in the western district had reached some sort of an understanding with Japanese gendarmes whereby Chinese in the blockaded area might have freedom of moving into the Settlement proper to obtain their food and other things provided they have their "guarantors". As a result, more than 1,000 of them signed with relief yesterday afternoon when they were allowed to go. It was stated that many Chinese might be thus allowed to go free today so as to prevent their starving as much as possible while still abiding with the Japanese in their precautionary vigilance.

1940
Situation In Blockaded
Western Area Eases As

Foreign Pedestrian And Vehicular Traffic Is Being

CHINESE RESIDENTS FACE STARVATION
AS ALL FOOD SUPPLIES EXHAUSTED

Although the situation in the Western District of Shanghai was somewhat eased yesterday afternoon the blockade of the area imposed by Japanese Gendarmes after the shooting of Private Sazaki staged by a lone Chinese gunman on Saturday was still being enforced yesterday with no Chinese being admitted or permitted to leave the blockaded district.

Foreigners yesterday afternoon, however, were permitted to leave and enter the district by way of the Tifeng and Great Western Roads intersection where all foreign pedestrian and vehicular traffic was being inspected by Japanese Gendarmes and City Government policemen.

Chinese caught in the blockaded zone were frantic yesterday as unable to leave the area no food supplies were available to them, all stocks kept in the district being exhausted.

Despite the rigidity of the blockade being loosened residents of various blind alleys along Yu Yuen Road were still unable to leave their houses as barbed wire entanglements placed in the entrances of these lanes were still standing intact. Enterprising Chinese pedlars, however, were reported to be managing to bring in food to these stranded residents charging them exorbitant prices.

The Yu Yuen Road barricade shifted towards the Paramount Hotel yesterday afternoon was still closed to all pedestrians except to foreign school children going to the various public schools in the district. Despite the fact that teachers of the public schools were requested earlier in the day to present identification papers issued to them by the Bubbling Well Police Station, Japanese Gendarmes at the barrier barely questioned the foreigners as to what school they belonged letting them in and out of the district without further ado.

Kinnear Road Partly Open

Courteous, English-speaking Japanese Gendarmes, however, refused all other foreigners irrespective of nationality traffic across the Yu Yuen Road barrier requesting them to enter the zone by either Kinnear or Tifeng Roads. Chinese, it was learnt, had to be in possession of some sort of identification papers before access to the district was granted at the Kinnear Road barricade.

Contrary to previous days when barriers have been shifted around and no direct information could be obtained as to where pedestrians were allowed to enter all Japanese Gendarmes on duty near the barriers were informing foreign and Chinese pedestrians as to what possible course they should take for entry; exit, however, still being forbidden to Chinese except at the Kinnear Road barrier.

The barrier erected at Bubbling Well Road some 10 yards west of the Ford Hire Station at the St. George's square still remained closed throughout the day yesterday while another barricade on Tifeng Road near the Jessfield Road intersection was also barred to both foreigners and Chinese with the exception of school children who were allowed to proceed in and out. Chinese children attending S.M.C. schools in the blockaded zone were allowed in and out through the Tifeng Road/Jessfield Road and the Tifeng Road/Great Western Road barricades.

Inside the blockaded area all shops still remained closed with a few Chinese flags fluttering over deserted streets, patrols of Japanese Gendarmes and City Government plainclothesmen continuing their search of residences. Rifles levelled, pistols ominously placed on the ready patrols could be seen walking along Yu Yuen Road halting all Chinese for searches.

A fleet of Japanese Military trucks could be seen entering the district with bags of rice and other foodstuffs but it could not be ascertained whether the foodstuffs were to be placed there for sale to the residents of the district or not.

Five telephone operators sealed up in the Shanghai Telephone Company Lucerne Exchange, it was learnt yesterday, were relieved with some new operators while some 70 Chinese operators in the exchange were still not being permitted to leave. Food supplies and everyday necessities, were constantly being brought to them in trucks and no interference on the part of the sentries was reported.

Night Clubs Open

Local foreigners who frequent dining and dancing establishments in the Western District, particularly in the immediate vicinity of Jessfield Park, are not being denied the pleasure of patronizing their favourite places, there being two open routes to the Jessfield Park area. Foreigners may motor out Jessfield Road from the Paramount, thence out Kinnear Road to Edinburgh Road and out Yu Yuen Road. Or they may drive directly out Avenue Haig to Keswick Road and thence in Yu Yuen Road.

The immediate vicinity of the park boasts such important night clubs as the Bolero, Ali Baba, Jessfield, Roxy, Maybe and the Winter Garden.

P. Scheel And
HidakaConfer
On Blockade

Nippon Consul-General
Pledges Aid To Ease
Up Inconveniences

NO DEFINITE END OF
BLOCKADE SEEN

With a promise to look into the difficulties and inconveniences suffered by the foreign residents in the blockaded zone in the Western Area, entailed by the intensive house-to-house search for the killer of Private Sazaki for the last three days, Mr. Tateki Hidaka, Japanese Consul-General, stated that the blockade was impelled by necessity, in a conference with Mr. Poul Scheel, Senior Member of the Consular Body, at 10.30 yesterday morning at the Japanese Consulate.

Mr. Scheel, accompanied by Mr. H. E. Long, Secretary of the Consular Body, called on the Japanese Consul-General to discuss several issues arising from the protracted blockade, especially with regard to the inconveniences imposed upon the foreigners who reside in the area affected.

In the meeting, the Senior Consul expressed his sympathetic understanding of the Japanese authorities in instituting the measure and roundly condemned the atrocities perpetrated by gangsters in the Western District which have caused untold difficulties to those living there. Mr. Long told press representatives yesterday afternoon.

Safeguarding Of Rights

At the same time, it was pointed out, Mr. Scheel asked that steps be taken with a view to safeguarding the extraterritorial rights of the foreign residents. At this juncture, Mr. Long explained, the Senior Consul stressed the fact that responsibility for the murder of the Japanese Gendarme was placed on certain Chinese elements.

It is understood that the Japanese Consul-General promised to look into the matter of transporting food, medicines, and other extreme necessities for foreigners and foreign institutions in the blockaded zone. Arrangements looking towards the transportation of sick persons, government employees and school children in and out of the cordoned area without much inconvenience were also requested by the Senior Consul, Mr. Long indicated.

Mr. Hidaka, it was stated, explained that the extraordinary measure in the Western District was taken in order that a thorough search could be made of all the houses where the culprit or culprits might possible be hiding the weapon used in the shooting affray.

Search Of Cars Explained

Explaining why motor cars have been searched even if they belonged to foreigners, Mr. Hidaka said that the gun used in the killing might have been conveniently put in any part of the car without the knowledge of the owner, Mr. Long stated.

The possibility of a foreigner being in league with the culprit was also hinted in the statement of Mr. Hidaka, Mr. Long elucidated, when he explained the necessity of having foreigners regulated in going in and coming out of the restricted zone.

While he promised to help in getting the restrictions eased up, the Japanese Consul-General did not indicate how long the blockade would last, Mr. Long concluded.

(United Press)
PEIPING, Nov. 30.—The Chinese population and especially those residing near the Japanese military headquarters continued today to fear possible stern measures as a result of the murder by a Chinese yesterday of a Japanese Army lieutenant-colonel.

An increase in food prices was expected because immediately after the shooting the Japanese closed all city gates in an effort to trap the assassin.

The Japanese colonel was being conveyed to the Japanese military headquarters inside the city walls about noon yesterday when he was shot dead.

The Japanese immediately closed all gates and cordoned the area of the shooting and started searching thousands of Chinese. SP. BR. REGISTRY

Another Japanese Shot
In “Badlands” Area

Whole District Blockaded As Troops Launch
Rigorous Search for Assassin; Gendarmes
Open Fire in Vain on Fleeing Gunman

SHANGHAI'S "badlands" were placed under blockade by Japanese troops for the second time within less than two months yesterday afternoon when an unidentified gunman opened fire on a group of three Japanese gendarmes, seriously wounded one of them, and then made good his escape despite a burst of gunfire blazed from the pistols of the injured man's two unharmed colleagues.

Victim of the shooting once again was a corporal, the second of his rank to have fallen from gun wounds in that area, but Japanese authorities last night refused to disclose his name. Previously shot in the "badlands" area was Corporal Sato also of the gendarmerie, who was mortally wounded as he was walking through a village just to the north of Yu Yuen Road, seven weeks ago.

A Chinese pedestrian also was wounded during yesterday's affray, which took place at about 2.20 p.m., near Lane 52, off Great Western Road. Immediately after the shooting, Japanese gendarmerie in full field kit, and large numbers of police from the Municipality of Greater Shanghai were rushed to the scene in trucks and flung barbed wire barricades across all roads leading westwards from the Settlement proper.

Consternation reigned among the residents of the western district, particularly when at various points foreigners as well as Chinese were refused passage either way through the barriers. Judging by the varied restrictions enforced from time to time, it appeared either that the troops themselves were without definite instructions on the subject, or that the search was being shifted from area to area.

Barriers Shifted

This was demonstrated by the fact that between 3 p.m. and 6.30 p.m. Great Western Road was blockaded to both Chinese and foreigners, while Yu Yuen Road was blockaded to Chinese only, foreigners being permitted to proceed from the Tifeng Road intersection on foot.

At 7.30 p.m., however, Yu Yuen Road was placed under complete blockade, neither foreigners nor Chinese being permitted to pass the barriers until 10.30 p.m. At a later hour last night, whereas foreigners were allowed to pass on foot along Great Western Road.

Fears were immediately aroused among Chinese residents that the blockade would become as rigorous as it was following the shooting of Corporal Sato, and until darkness there was a run on food shops as stocks were laid in.

Other Attacks Recalled

While it was generally recalled that the shooting in Great Western Road yesterday was but one of a series of attacks which have been made on Japanese in Japanese-occupied areas, and that the attempted assassination may have been carried out as a "patriotic" protest against the recognition of Mr. Wang Ching-wei's government by the Japanese Government, it was also pointed out that this was the first attack which had been made on a Japanese subject since the appointment of Mr. Chen Kung-pao as Mayor of Greater Shanghai.

Mr. Chen, it was pointed out, had threatened to "clean up" Shanghai's western crime area upon his appointment, and there recently had been noticed a decided increase in the number of Japanese Special Service Section men operating in the district.

In defiance of Mr. Chen's threat, however, a number of new gambling houses had been opened in the western district, and Settlement police circles were of the belief that the "guards" attached to these houses were attempting to intimidate Mr. Chen before he began his campaign.

It was indicated last night that there would be an increase in restrictions by the Japanese authorities in the western district today as the result of yesterday's shooting, and although police authorities were non-committal on the subject, it was hinted that there might be a complete dislocation of traffic in that area.

ON THE WHANGPOO

On December 1, explosions took place in two
Japanese tugs which were anchored in the Japanese Naval Dockyard
on the Whangpoo. As the Japanese kept it secret, outside
circles did not know of this occurrence. Now, according to
detailed information given by workers of the wharfs at that

tugs loaded with ammunition and other military supplies arrived
on November 29 in the vicinity of the wharf of the Japanese

ten employees of the Kiangnan Dockyard were seriously injured.

afterwards, but no arrest was made. It is learned that the

ASSASSINATION OF JUDGE D'HOOGHE, FRENCH MUNICIPAL ADVOCATE

At 7.15 p.m. yesterday, Judge D'Hooghe,
French Municipal Advocate, was fatally shot on Route de
Boissezon in the French Concession.
Judge D'Hooghe and his family lived in Room 34
in a foreign apartment house at No. 24 Route de Boissezon.
At 8 a.m. every day he went to his office in the French
Municipal Council and returned to his apartment at about
6 p.m. in his private motor car (Licence No.641).
After returning to his apartment from his
office yesterday afternoon, Judge D'Hooghe left his room
and went downstairs at 7.15 p.m. intending to go to a
dinner party. As he approached his private motor car
which was parked in front of the apartment, two men
suddenly appeared from the roadside and fired five or six
shots; two bullets struck him in the head and one took
effect in the waist. Judge D'Hooghe collapsed. Seeing
that they had attained their aim, the gunmen made good
their escape.
Upon receipt of a report, the French Police
sent out a large party of detectives and policemen in
Police vans and a search was made for the gunmen, but
without success. Judge D'Hooghe was immediately removed
to St. Marie Hospital. At 8 p.m. an operation was
performed, but due to his advanced age, the Judge succumbed
to his serious wounds at 8.35 p.m.
Judge D'Hooghe was 65 years of age at the time
of his death. He came to China a number of years ago,
and was once Presiding Judge in the now defunct Mixed
Court in the French Concession. He had held his present
position for 14 years.
The French Police are investigating the
cause of the assassination.

In connection with the interference with the Chinese watchmen and the compulsory enforcement of an order compelling ricsha coolies to take out licences in the Western District by the Japanese gendarmes, negotiations were opened with the Japanese authorities by the S.M.C. yesterday. According to an official statement issued by the Publicity Office of the S.M.C., a letter has been sent to the Japanese Consul-General calling his attention to both matters.

The blockade has resulted in considerable impairment of the monopolistic rights of traffic in the Western District enjoyed by the International Settlement. The operation of Japanese-owned buses on Yu Yuen Road and Great Western Road has given rise to much inconvenience and annoyance to the Settlement authorities and the residents. Since yesterday morning, the blockade has been lifted. According to reliable quarters, the blockade was lifted due to either of the following grounds:-
(1) Since the blockade, the China Club on Great Western Road and the Hwa Loh Club (花樂會) on Yu Yuen Road, both being large gambling dens, have suffered considerable losses. Consequently, they have offered a huge sum as a passage money. Though the exact amount is unknown, it is said to be somewhere round $500,000.
(2). Though the Japanese have not yet disclosed the result of their purge in the cesspool of terroristic elements at Waung Ka Loong and Edinburgh Road, they have now considered it unnecessary to blockade so large an area. Consequently, the outer regions have been reopened but Waung Ka Loong, etc. were still closed yesterday.

At about 11 a.m. yesterday, a couple of buses each of the Routes No. 1 and 9 of the China General Omnibus Company resumed operations on Yu Yuen Road; in the afternoon Route No. 9 buses and Route No. 20 railless cars likewise resumed operations along Great Western Road and Yu Yuen Road. None of the so-called Western District People's buses were noticed travelling in the Western District yesterday. It is said that the loss suffered by the China General Omnibus Co. and the Shanghai Tramway Co. amounted altogether to approximately $80,000. Meanwhile, ricshas bearing Settlement licences are still denied entrance into the outlying roads area, unless they are issued with "City Government licences" or have affixed on the back the characters "with special permission from the Western District Traffic Committee."

In connection with the illegal operation of Japanese-owned buses in the blockaded area in the Western District, a protest was lodged with the Japanese Consul-General by the S.M.C. at beginning of this week, but no reply has yet been received by the Council to its protest. However, it is generally expected that the Japanese-owned buses will cease operations in the area because it has already been declared by the Japanese authorities that this operation was but a temporary arrangement.

December 15, 1940. Morning Translation.

The cause of the reopening is unknown. However,
a study of the reports appearing in local newspapers
previously and of the statistics of the "remarkable
performances" conducted during the period of the blockade,
will offer no difficulty in understanding the cause of the
blockade.

According to Press reports, pedestrians
desiring passage were required to pay a "passage money"
ranging from $0.20 to $0.50. In all the blockade lasted
14 days. If it is taken into account that every day only
1,000 pedestrians were given passage in this manner, the
sum acquired would have been quite considerable.

"Japanese-owned buses are operating along Yu
Yuen Road and are doing quite good business." "The routes
of the British-owned buses have all been shortened and
have stopped travelling in the blockaded area." These are
two other headings appearing in newspapers. It is needless
to point out the facts as the readers must have already
understood them well.

According to them, the blockade was enforced
because they desired to effect the arrest of the culprits.
However, by common sense, in view of the fact that a number
of places in the blockaded area had been reopened and closed
several times during the blockade, it seems unlikely that
they could have been so foolish as to endeavour to effect
the apprehension of the culprits after the reopening of
the place.

According to a report appearing in this paper,
the China Club has already offered a sum of $500,000 to a
certain party as "protection fee" and the blockade would
soon be lifted.

Now the blockaded area has been reopened. All
the facts surrounding this blockade have shown the true
description of the master of the "new order."

TIRIKU SHIMPO :-

REFUTATION OF EXAGGERATED REPORTS

Foreign newspapers and anti-Japanese
Chinese newspapers in the Settlements are publishing
exaggerated reports to incite the people against the joint
action taken in the Western District by Japan and China
towards lawless elements. It is alleged that as a
result of the blockade of the district, the residents
there are suffering from acute shortage of foodstuffs
while the China Bus Company and the Tramway Company are
sustaining an enormous loss. But actually, conditions
in the District are totally different from what these
newspapers say.
As for the Western District People's
Omnibus Company, it is established by leading persons in
the blockaded area and is operating its buses on Yu Yuen
Road and Great Western Road thereby considerably
alleviating traffic congestion.
Although the China Bus Company and
the Tramway Company are strongly criticizing the alleged
encroachment upon their rights, they have taken advantage
of the disorder and confusion created by the former
Shanghai Incident and acquired the right to run their
buses and trams in this District in defiance of the strong
objection raised by the Chinese side. On these grounds,
they have no basis on which to lay their claim for their
legal rights.

National Herald (comment) :-

ABANDONMENT OF THE APPEASEMENT POLICY

Since the outlying road areas have been blockaded, the transportation franchise granted by the S.M.C. has been violated and policemen have been assaulted and insulted. A certain party is again trying to collect ricsha licence fees. Last night, a Route No. 7 bus was attacked on Edinburgh Road.
A foreign observer has declared that this was a planned and organized attempt of the Japanese to partition the administrative rights of the S.M.C. in the Western District, with the object of tearing up the Yangkingpang Land Regulations.
As regards the infringement of the transportation franchise, the S.M.C. opened negotiations the day before yesterday. With reference to the assaulting and insulting of policemen, it is said that a protest will be delivered to-day. It is not known what the reply of the Japanese will be.
As the S.M.C. is an executive organization formed according to the Yangkingpang Land Regulations, it seems that the S.M.C. should not permit the Japanese to break the Regulations. The S.M.C. should abandon its long-adopted appeasement policy and open strong negotiations with the Japanese. Should it fail, the S.M.C. must ask the Consular Body and the foreign governments concerned for assistance, so as to bring the matter to the attention of the Japanese Government.

CONDITIONS IN THE WESTERN DISTRICT
It was learned by a reporter of this paper
that the situation in the blockaded area in the Western
District became worse yesterday. Traffic from Edinburgh
Road to Avenue Haig was again interrupted, while Great
Western Road and other places are still under blockade.
Pedestrians are complaining for they have to make a long
detour. Business in the Farrens Club was bad yesterday. It
is said that patriotic slogans were discovered yesterday
written on the walls of the Li Chao Fang (李兆坊) alleyway
off Yu Yuen Road. A search was conducted by the Japanese
soldiers, but it had no result. The Japanese gendarmes and
mercenary policemen are continuing to search Chinese residences.
Yesterday some ten primary school students
inside Lane 909, Yu Yuen Road, were noticed throwing
newspapers at one another. The Japanese gendarmes examined
the newspapers and found that all these newspapers were
supporters of justice. Becoming angry, the Japanese tried to
arrest the students, but the latter escaped. The gendarmes
knocked at the doors of the houses in the alleyway with the
object of carrying out a search but when they found that they
could not do anything, they blockaded the alleyway. As their
food supplies are running out, the residents are in danger
of starvation.
Another report states that the British-owned
buses which have been running in the Western District were
suddenly attacked by a large number of bad elements. A Route
No. 7 bus which had stopped at a terminus near the corner of
Edinburgh Road and Avenue Haig was attacked by a number of
bad elements who threw bricks and tiles into the bus. The
driver and conductor of the bus remonstrated, but no heed
was paid to them. The driver, Yi Zung-yien (易人化), aged
37, native of Anhwei, residing at No. 5, Zung Teh Li
(仁德里), Brenan Road, was injured on the head and was sent
to the Red Cross Hospital. It is believed that the bad elements
had been instigated into carrying out such activities with the
object of harming the interests of foreigners.
According to information secured from
foreign sources, the S.M.C. did not lodge a protest yesterday
with the Japanese authorities against the assault of a Chinese
Police Officer of the S.M.P. by Japanese gendarmes. According
to a spokesman of the Council, a protest may be handed to the
Japanese this morning.
As regards the operation of Japanese-owned
buses in the Western District, the Chairman of the S.M.C.
opened negotiations with the Japanese Consul-General on
December 10.
It was learned by a reporter of the Dah
Chung News Agency that this matter was discussed at the Council
meeting yesterday afternoon. It is said that after it had
made an investigation, the Japanese Consulate replied that
Japanese official circles were unaware of the matter as the
running of the Japanese-owned buses in the Western District
was an individual act.
It is said that negotiations will be opened,
while the Japanese Councillors will be asked to make an
investigation into this affair.

"CHINESE POLICEMEN IN FRENCH CONCESSION ON STRIKE YESTERDAY
MORNING ; 17 DEMANDS FOR BETTER TREATMENT SUBMITTED ;
AUTHORITIES PROMISE TO GIVE REPLY WITHOUT 3 OR 4 DAYS"

The entire body of Chinese policemen in the
French Concession, who are finding it difficult to maintain
their livelihood with their small pay, recently submitted,
verbally, to the French authorities a demand for an increase
of wages. As no formal reply has been given by the French
authorities, 150 Chinese policemen of Lokawei Police Station
went on strike at 8.45 a.m. yesterday and their action was
followed by the 140 Chinese policemen in other Stations.
As a result of the strike, traffic in the
French Concession was in great disorder as no policemen were
on traffic duty, but the situation improved after employees
of the French Tramway Company and French policemen took over
the traffic duty.
The Commissioner and Deputy Commissioner of
the French Police immediately held a conference with the
Chinese policemen of Lokawei Station. 120 Chinese policemen
were present.
The Commissioner of the French Police stated
the French authorities were paying attention to the liveli-
hood of the Chinese policemen owing to the sharp increases
in the prices of commodities and that measures for their
better treatment were already under consideration. The
Commissioner then asked the Chinese policemen on strike to
submit their demands.
Chinese policemen Nos. 158, 164 and 598 were
then elected representatives of the policemen and they
handed the demands to the Commissioner.
The Commissioner stated that he would give
guarantee a satisfactory reply to the strikers within three
or four days and expressed the hope that the Chinese policemen,
would, for the sake of peace and good order, immediately
resume duty.
The strikers were satisfied with the
Commissioner's promise and resumed duty at once.
Yesterday morning, a Chinese policeman
propagating a strike at the corner of Route Stanislas
Chevalier and Rue Massenet was arrested by white Russian
detectives but he was released before the Chinese policemen
on strike resumed duty.
The following are the demands submitted by
the entire body of Chinese policemen:-
(1) The formation of a French Concession
Chinese Policemen's Mutual Aid Association.

We distinctly recall that when shooting cases were occurring repeatedly in the two Foreign Settlements, the Japanese strongly criticized the inefficiency of the Police Forces of the Foreign Settlements and suggested that Japanese be allowed to maintain peace and good order in the Foreign Settlements.
Of late many cases of assassination have taken place in Hongkew and in the Western District where peace and good order is being maintained by Japanese. Furthermore, the victims in these cases were Japanese army or naval officers. What is stranger still is that ten unsolved cases have occurred and in each case the assailant or assailants had been able to make good their escape.
From this one may come to the conclusion that the Japanese troops and the mercenary police who are so skillful in maintaining peace and good order have failed to solve these cases and can only shake their heads and sigh.
Of late, the Japanese seemed to have become wiser. They have resorted to the method of blockading an area. They may blockade Hongkew to-day and the Western District to-morrow; but the people living in these areas have to undergo indescribable suffering. At first mercenary policemen would resort to extortion and this would be followed by the running of buses operated by Japanese. However, they seem to have overlooked the point that after all the people have removed, there would be no peace and good order to be maintained. In that event, they would only have the work of protecting themselves.

Chinese-American Daily News, Cheng Yien Pao, Sin Wan Pao, Shun
Pao, National Herald :-

CONSULAR BODY OPENS NEGOTIATIONS OVER BLOCKADE OF
WESTERN DISTRICT

Following the shooting of a Japanese gendarme
on Great Western Road in the Western District on November 30,
the Japanese authorities immediately blockaded an area
bounded by Tifeng Road, Great Western Road, Edinburgh Road
and Yu Yuen Road. Both Chinese and foreign residents
living in the blockaded areas were prohibited from leaving.
On the evening of December 2, the Japanese
extended the blockade to the front of the Paramount Ballroom
and barbed wire barricades were placed on the border of
the Settlement. The 100,000 residents living in the
blockaded areas are faced with difficulties of securing
food supplies.

It is said that the S.M.C. has opened
negotiations with the Japanese. According to Major Bourne,
Commissioner of S.M.P., the negotiations held on the
morning of December 3 for the immediate removal of the
blockade had no result, but measures were drawn up restricting
the movements of Chinese and foreign residents, but they
were less severe in character.

On December 3, Japanese soldiers and gendarmes
and Chinese policemen with fixed bayonets patrolled the
blockaded areas in the Western District. Chinese people
were prohibited from leaving or entering nor were foodstuffs
allowed to be sent in. It was said that teachers and
students would be permitted free access, but this has been
found to be untrue. Foreigners are permitted to pass the
barricades.

Large and small gambling dens and shops in
the blockaded areas are all closed. The price of rice
in the area has been increased considerably.

Out of consideration for the safety of the
Chinese and foreign residents in the blockaded area,
the S.M.C. opened negotiations with the Japanese on the
morning of December 3 with the object of procuring freedom
of access for the residents. In the meantime, the Senior
Consul has been requested to open negotiations with the
Japanese Consul-General so that an early settlement of the
trouble might be found.

The Senior Consul says that the Japanese
Consul-General is in sympathy with the residents, but in
his letter of reply, received at 2 p.m. that day,
he states that the restrictions have been adopted in
order to facilitate the arrest of the murderers and that
the blockade would not be removed until such time as
the Japanese authorities come to the conclusion that
it would be impossible to arrest the murderers.

The Japanese Police officer assisting in the
negotiations says that the reply received from the
Japanese authorities indicates that the blockade would
not be removed for some time to come and that there is
even a possibility of the blockade being continued for
two or three weeks.

Central China Daily News, Kuo Min Daily News, New China Daily
News and Bing Pao :-

Conditions In The Western District

The Western District area has been blockaded
for four days. The food question in the area is gradually
becoming acute. Yesterday, as a result of a consultation
between the Western District Police and the Japanese, the
food situation was a little better. Yesterday, the Japanese
and the Western District Police decided to issue to residents
in the area temporary passes to enter or leave the area
between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. every day. Those who can procure
shop guarantee can apply for this temporary permission at
the outpost of the Western District Police Bureau, Siao Zar
Kiao (小 不 桥 ). It is learned that yesterday several
thousand people secured such permits. The issuing of permits
will continue for two days. It was temporarily arranged
that people in Zien Ka Hong and Wang Ka Loong will be
allowed to pass. Simultaneously Yu Yuen and Tifeng Roads
were also partly opened. Foreigners are allowed to enter
or leave the area freely.

Chinese-American Daily News (comment) :-

The Blockaded "Happy Land"

The severe blockade of "Happy Land" in the
Shanghai Western District as a result of the shooting of
a Japanese gendarme on Great Western Road entered its fifth
day to-day. Judging by the undermentioned three minor
cases, one can imagine the discomfort and hardship that is
being experienced by the people living inside the blockaded
area :-
(1) A Chinese woman who works in a foreign
family in the French Concession but who lives in the
blockaded area has five children. On ordinary days she
used to return home after her work, but since Saturday last
she has not been able to visit her children. She is wild
with anxiety as there is no food left in the house.
(2) As they were late in leaving school on
Saturday last, six Chinese students, their ages varying
from 6 to 10, have been confined in the premises of the
S.M.C. Public School on Edinburgh Road with five teachers.
They are living on biscuits and sleep on wooden benches,
sharing three or four blankets with their five teachers.
(3) The 85 Chinese and foreign girl telephone
operators at the Lucerne Exchange, who had spent almost 60
hours at their posts since the enforcement of the blockade
and who had had only four hours sleep, were relieved by a
new shift yesterday morning.
Notwithstanding the negotiations opened by
the Consular Body and the S.M.C. with the Japanese
authorities for the lifting of the blockade and that
permission be given for food supplies to be sent into
the blockaded area, the Japanese authorities do not seem
willing to remove the blockade until the culprit is
apprehended. If the Japanese authorities insist on this,
